episodes.summary: Describes growing up in a wooden house by the river in Iloilo, built by her father.
places: little wooden house beside the river

episodes.summary: Explains the house was on tall posts to avoid flooding during the rainy season.
Recalls her childhood perception of the river as a friendly neighbor.
Describes the layout of the house, including two rooms, a kitchen, and a bamboo porch.
Recalls all six children sleeping together in one room under a mosquito net.
Describes the morning sunlight coming through the gaps in the house and drawing stripes on the floor.
Describes her mother's kitchen and her early morning routine of cooking rice and preparing cakes for the market.
Recalls her father keeping his tools under the house and her watching him work on boats.
Describes the mango tree in front of the house and her brother Nestor climbing it.
Recalls the family keeping chickens, a pig, and a rooster named General who chased her to the well every morning.
Describes the well shared by four families and the gossip exchanged there while fetching water.
Recalls the typhoon season, the family's preparations, and their fear during the storm.
Describes a night when the river flooded the house, forcing the family to take shelter in the attic.
Recalls the aftermath of the flood, including cleaning the house and the lingering smell of wet earth.
Describes the neighbors gathering on the porch after supper to talk and share palm wine.
Recalls the children chasing fireflies along the riverbank with empty jam jars.
Describes her grandmother sitting in her rocking chair, chewing betel nut, humming, and teaching her to sew.
Recalls the house having no electricity until she was nine, and the family's reaction to the first light bulb.
Reflects on her memories of the house in Iloilo, even while living in Abu Dhabi.
Recalls her mother's Sunday chicken adobo cooking process and the family's anticipation.
time_references: when father came home early from the water

episodes.summary: Describes the family eating adobo together on the porch, with her father giving her the chicken thigh.
Reflects on the taste of adobo the next day and her mother's wisdom about life.
Recalls bringing coconut vinegar to Abu Dhabi and the first time cooking adobo there.
time_references: when I moved to Abu Dhabi

episodes.summary: Describes finding the right vinegar in Abu Dhabi and her children's love for her adobo.
Reflects on using a pressure cooker and the nostalgia tied to cooking adobo.
Hopes her children will carry on the tradition of cooking adobo after she is gone.
Begins school at age six in a one-story school near the Iloilo market with a red tin roof and a muddy yard.
Walks to school barefoot with sisters, carrying books tied with a rubber strap.
Mother irons her white blouse and polishes her black shoes, which she carries in a cloth bag and puts on at the school gate.
Describes first teacher, Missus Dayrit, as a round woman with a voice like a church bell and a long wooden pointer.
Sits three to a desk on worn benches, loves the smell of chalk dust and the squeak of the blackboard.
Learns to write in copybooks with blue lines and a rooster on the cover, and her neat handwriting is pinned on the wall by Missus Dayrit.
Trips over a goat on the way home after her handwriting is praised.
Describes morning routine at school: standing in rows, singing the anthem, stretching arms, and reciting multiplication tables.
Arithmetic is her best subject, but she loves stories most; Missus Dayrit teaches singing, mostly about rain and rice.
The school library is one shelf in a cupboard that smells of mildew; she reads every book twice, including a thick one about the stars.
At lunchtime, sits under the acacia tree with tin boxes of rice; Jun trades his dried fish for her sweet rice cake.
On rainy days, the teacher lets them tell stories, and she discovers people listen when she uses her hands.
Draws the principal with a fish for a nose in her notebook, Tess laughs and falls off the bench, and they are sent to stand in the corner.
Mother hears about the incident and gives her a look worse than any scolding, then laughs because she cannot stay angry.
At the school fiesta, she stars in a play about a girl who saves her village, wearing a crown of banana leaves and a cape made from a curtain.
Forgets her lines in the play, makes up new ones, and the audience claps; decides she wants to stand in front of a room and talk.
Describes the school's condition after the war: torn books, patched walls, but teachers treated every child as a future doctor and gave them hope.
Reflects on becoming a teacher and trying to give the same gift of hope to every child.
Even now, the smell of chalk reminds her of being six years old with tight braids.
In dry months, plays tag until dust turns uniforms brown; wishes to go back for one more morning with the anthem and multiplication tables.
Introduces her childhood friend Tess, who lived nearby and was known for her gap-toothed whistle.
Recalls the day Tess fell into the river and the narrator fished her out, making her feel like a hero.
Describes daily activities with Tess, including collecting shells, trading them, and catching crabs.
Recalls teaching Tess to read using tin can labels and Tess's mother selling fish at the market.
Describes Saturdays spent helping their mothers and making corn husk dolls together.
Recalls the secret hiding spot under the mango tree where they kept a biscuit tin with treasures.
Describes Tess's dream of becoming a singer and the narrator's dream of becoming a teacher.
Recalls Tess's family moving to Bacolod and the emotional farewell.
Describes the loneliness after Tess left and the fading of their letter-writing.
Recalls receiving a postcard from Tess years later, revealing she became a church singer.
Describes revisiting Iloilo and finding the mango tree gone, replaced by a concrete house.
Reflects on singing in her church choir in Abu Dhabi and thinking of Tess.
Shares her belief that Tess is still out there singing and that good friends are never truly lost.
Begins working at Madame Lim's dressmaker's shop at sixteen on Saturdays to help pay for books.
Describes the physical layout and atmosphere of Madame Lim's shop.
Introduces Madame Lim's appearance and personality.
Recalls her first task of sorting buttons and Madame Lim's reasoning behind it.
Describes being promoted to sewing hems and her pride in the work.
Describes the fabrics and sensory details of the shop.
Recalls learning to sew through trial and error, including pricking her fingers.
Describes her pay and how she divided it between her mother and herself.
Describes her coworkers and their interactions, including Aling Pacita's singing and Remedios's wedding.
Reflects on the lessons learned from the job, including patience and understanding people.
Recalls Madame Lim's diplomacy with a difficult customer.
Describes the shop's challenges during typhoon season.
Recalls working at the shop for two years until leaving for teachers college.
Describes Madame Lim's farewell gift of silver scissors and her advice about teaching.
Reflects on keeping the scissors and the lasting impact of the job.
Shares the broader lessons and pride from her first job.
Introduces her husband Ramon as the most important person in her life.
Describes meeting Ramon at church on a rainy Sunday when she was 22 and he was 25.
Recalls Ramon walking her home and describing his travels as a ship's cook.
Describes Ramon courting her for two years with letters from around the world.
Recalls Ramon cooking for her family and winning her parents' approval.
Describes their wedding in the same church where they met, including dropping the ring.
Reflects on the challenges of being married to a seafarer for nearly thirty years.
Describes Ramon's gentle nature and how he handled a crashed motorbike incident.
Recalls Ramon retiring and the adjustments of living together full-time.
Describes Ramon's current hobby of growing herbs and their evening routine.
Reflects on why their marriage lasted, attributing it to the letters they exchanged.
Describes Ramon's hands now and her enduring love for him.
Shares her belief that a good marriage is built on patience and a hot meal.
Recalls the day she left Iloilo for Abu Dhabi in 1992, with her family seeing her off at the airport.
Grace recalls planning her daughter Liza's wedding in Abu Dhabi, which took a year and involved two cultures.
Grace describes sewing sixteen yellow silk gowns for the flower girls, which left her fingers sore and pins scattered everywhere.
Ramon and his brother cooked for four days, preparing pancit and lechon for the wedding.
Grace reflects on the morning of the wedding, feeling emotional while helping Liza into her gown.
Grace describes the wedding ceremony, including her choir singing and Ramon walking Liza down the aisle.
Grace describes the wedding reception, including the garden setting, karaoke, and dancing.
Grace reflects on the end of the wedding party, sharing a quiet moment with Ramon and Liza.
Grace reflects on the wedding as a celebration of unity between two families and cultures.
Grace expresses her hope that she will remember the sensory details of the wedding, like the smell of jasmine and roasted pig, as she grows older.
Grace introduces Missus Ledesma, the principal of her first school, describing her appearance and weekly attire.
Grace recalls her first day of teaching at 22, struggling with a lesson plan and losing the children's attention.
Missus Ledesma observes Grace's teaching and gently critiques her for focusing on the plan instead of the children.
Missus Ledesma invites Grace to her office, shares her own first-day teaching disaster, and they bond over laughter.
Missus Ledesma teaches Grace to engage children with creativity, such as turning fractions into a cake-sharing story.
Missus Ledesma brings a live crab to class, which escapes and causes chaos, leaving a lasting impression on Grace.
Missus Ledesma emphasizes noticing quiet children and keeps a notebook with positive observations about each child weekly.
Missus Ledesma helps a struggling student, Ernesto, learn to read with patience and flashcards, leading to his public reading success.
time_references: by the end of the year

episodes.summary: Missus Ledesma values order and punctuality, believing it fosters safety and bravery in children.
Grace tells Missus Ledesma about her plan to move abroad, and Missus Ledesma gives her an orchid to take with her.
Grace honors Missus Ledesma after her death by lighting a candle and singing her favorite hymn in Abu Dhabi.
Grace reflects on the orchids she grows, descendants of the one Missus Ledesma gave her, and remembers her mentor fondly.
Grace shares Missus Ledesma's lessons with new teachers, emphasizing the importance of seeing the children in the room.
Grace expresses gratitude for Missus Ledesma's mentorship and the lasting impact it had on her teaching career.
Grace recalls a memorable boat journey with her father to deliver a fishing boat to Guimaras Island when she was ten.
